extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) evaluating written description under 35 U.S.C. 112
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a patent application's specification adequately describes the claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (the written description requirement), including special considerations for biological, chemical, genus/species, means-plus-function, and priority/claim-amendment issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental written description test
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that the applicant was in possession of the invention as of the filing date? (e.g., "does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed"; Vas-Cath, Gosteli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective standard: whether the disclosure 'reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.' Consider entire specification (words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, by disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show the invention was complete, or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For biological materials, a deposit made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. (see 1.804 and 1.809) may evidence reduction to practice. Drawings alone can provide written description in some cases (citations: Vas-Cath, Wolfensperger, Autogiro).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (complete or partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation between function and structure) can show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for biomolecules: sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, length, unique cleavage by particular enzymes, isoelectric points, restriction enzyme maps, comparison of enzymatic activities, antibody cross-reactivity. Presence of such distinguishing characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from others is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional definition limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition by function alone 'does not suffice' to describe a coding sequence or other claimed subject matter unless coupled with known or disclosed correlation between function and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function-only recitations are often 'little more than a wish' (Eli Lilly, In re Wilder). In predictable arts where structure-function correlations exist, function + minimal structure may suffice (see Fonar for software).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical/structural precision requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention generally requires a precise definition (structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties), not merely a wish or plan for obtaining the chemical invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle held methods/assays without disclosure of actual compounds insufficient to describe claimed methods of selective inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6) claim support
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 6, it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; written description must support the means/step-plus-function limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must consider summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings in assessing support. Adequacy under para.1 is met if: (1) written description adequately links adequately described particular structure/material/acts to the recited function; or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would have known what structure/material/acts perform the recited function. See MPEP §2181 and supplemental guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or well-known matter
rubrics_metrics.description: What is conventional or well-known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be disclosed in detail in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written description requirement must be applied in context: as the field evolves, balance between what is known and what must be disclosed changes (Capon v. Eshhar). In mature technologies, less detail may be required; in unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single embodiment/species analysis procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species: (A) determine whether application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether reduction to drawings or structural formula sufficiently shows possession; (C) if not, determine whether other identifying characteristics sufficiently show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a complete structure (or acts of a process) is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species and rejection must not be made. See Fields v. Conover for lack of 'full, clear, concise, and exact' description examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete structure — alternative sufficiency analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complete structure is not disclosed, determine whether the specification discloses other relevant identifying characteristics sufficient that a skilled artisan would recognize applicant was in possession (e.g., function + well-established structure-function correlation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the art has a strong correlation between structure and function, one could predict structure from function with reasonable confidence; absent such correlation, function alone is generally insufficient (Eli Lilly, In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in possession determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination considering multiple factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Use patents and prior printed publications to gauge maturity of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claim written description (representative species) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect variation within the genus. When substantial variation exists, more species must be described. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus only if disclosure indicates patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number depends on predictability/skill in art
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes a 'representative number' is an inverse function of the skill and knowledge in the art; in predictable arts fewer species may suffice, in unpredictable arts more species are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disclosure of an amino acid sequence may support a genus of nucleic acids encoding it because the genetic code is known; contrast with unpredictable biotechnological arts where a single species often cannot support a genus (Enzo Biochem, Noelle v. Lederman).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-species disclosure may sometimes support genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure of only one species may support a genus if the disclosure indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or where the specification conveys that broader coverage is intended and enablement/predictability justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples: Rasmussen (one method supported 'adheringly applying' genus), Herschler (known chemical compounds in auxiliary use). But LizardTech and Tronzo show a single embodiment often cannot support expansive generic claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: New/amended claims and priority — examiner applicant burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: For new or amended claims or claims asserting earlier priority/filing date, the examiner has the initial burden to present evidence or reasoning why skilled persons would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the claimed invention; applicant should show support in the original disclosure for new/amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should specifically point out support for amendments (see MPEP §714.02 and §2163.06). Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported; absence of explicit limitation requires showing a POSA would understand the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's required findings when rejecting for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact to support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing date would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should suggest claim amendments when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, the examiner should suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application's written description, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Rasmussen and related precedents as guidance for suggesting allowable claim scope that aligns with disclosed embodiments/species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of applicant reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, re-determine patentability including written description in view of the whole record; if the record now demonstrates adequacy, do not repeat the rejection; if not, repeat rejection, fully respond to rebuttal, and thoroughly analyze affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner maintains the rejection, thoroughly analyze any affidavits relevant to the 112, para.1 written description requirement (see In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal wording not required but amended claims must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter of the claim need not be described literally to satisfy the written description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter not present in the application as filed, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or benefit of an earlier filing date denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If amended claims involve departure/addition/deletion from original disclosure, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described and take appropriate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between written description rejection and new matter objection
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of support in the original disclosure for claimed subject matter is addressed as a rejection under the written description requirement (35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph) or denial of priority; it should not be handled as an objection for new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New matter objections address amendments that attempt to add disclosure not originally presented; while analysis for both issues is similar, statutory bases and procedures differ (Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that each claim include all elements applicant described as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential or critical in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to claim an element the applicant described as essential can be grounds for rejecting new/child claims or denying priority (citations: Johnson Worldwide Associates, Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).
